item.content:encoded:
The Tonga Family Health Association ( TFHA ) has marked International Humanitarian Day in Nuku'alofa today with a focus on strengthening community resilience and ensuring humanitarian action upholds justice, dignity and equity.

TFHA executive director, Pelenatita Longopa, said the day called attention to the rising threats and attacks against aid workers and civilians, while calling for an end to impunity for violations of international humanitarian law.

Through its SPRINT IV Project, TFHA has positioned sexual and reproductive health ( SRH ) as a critical humanitarian priority, particularly during disasters when essential services can be disrupted or overlooked.

TFHA 's humanitarian work includes providing women, girls and vulnerable groups with access to mental health care, contraception and protection from gender-based violence.

Pelenatita Longopa said SRH was central to resilience because it protected the health and dignity of families during crises, empowered women and young people to participate in recovery and strengthened coordination between health, protection and communities.

Community representatives and humanitarians said humanitarian preparedness was a lived reality for Tonga, with the country's experience of volcanic eruptions and cyclones demonstrating the need for community-driven resilience.

The Civil Society Forum of Tonga also received donated humanitarian supplies from UN Global Medics, including hygiene packs and a water purifier intended to support families during future disasters.

The second half of the event featured a roundtable discussion involving humanitarian workers, volunteers, non-government organisations representatives and community members.

Discussions focused on how communities experienced and remembered the 2022 Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai volcanic eruption, including humanitarian challenges faced during the response.

Participants also examined lessons from the response, including what worked well, gaps in humanitarian coordination and challenges faced by agencies and communities.

The discussion also looked at the way forward, including how communities and service providers could strengthen disaster preparedness and resilience through strategic planning.

item.title: Tonga faces severe drought threat as El Niño brings very dry conditions nationwide

item.content:encoded:
Tonga is facing the prospect of a severe and prolonged drought, with the Tonga Meteorological Service warning that a strong to very strong El Niño could bring very dry conditions across the entire country and place growing pressure on water supplies, food production and public health.

The Meteorological Drought Outlook issued on 18 August 2026 says El Niño is already underway in Tonga and the tropical Pacific, with forecasts pointing to an event that could rank among the strongest observed since 1950. El Niño conditions typically bring below-average rainfall and the possibility of prolonged drought in Tonga.

The warning comes as Tonga is already experiencing widespread dryness. In July, dry conditions were observed across all of Tonga, with very dry conditions in Vava’u and seriously dry conditions in Tongatapu and ‘Eua. Over the three months from May to July, dry conditions were recorded across all island groups, with seriously dry conditions in Ha’apai, Tongatapu and ‘Eua.

The outlook for the coming months is even more concerning.

Very dry conditions are forecast across all of Tonga in August, with a 70 to 80 per cent chance in Niuafo’ou and Niuatoputapu, 50 to 70 per cent in Tongatapu and ‘Eua, and 40 to 50 per cent in Ha’apai and Vava’u.

For August to October, the chance of very dry conditions rises to between 80 and 100 per cent across all of Tonga.

The drought outlook shows the situation worsening in several island groups by the end of October. Niuafo’ou is forecast to move from Drought Alert to Drought Declaration, while Niuatoputapu is expected to remain under Drought Declaration after escalating from Drought Warning. Vava’u is forecast to progress from Drought Alert to Drought Declaration.

Ha’apai, Tongatapu and ‘Eua are already at Drought Declaration and are expected to remain there through October.

The outlook identifies reduced or empty water tanks within one month, followed by depleted groundwater, including on Tongatapu, and drying bore and well water. It also warns of increased costs for pumping and drinking water, as well as increased water salinity.

The impacts could become more severe if dry conditions persist, with competing demands for water from households, agriculture and livestock.

Agriculture is also expected to come under increasing pressure as soil moisture declines.

The Meteorological Service identifies impacts on yams, cassava and taro, along with reduced breadfruit and pineapple yields. Kava growth could be reduced, while cattle and pigs could also be affected by reduced pasture availability and increased demand for drinking water.

The outlook also warns of reduced crop production, higher crop prices, increased irrigation demand and impacts on livelihoods and food security.

The drought could also create serious health and hygiene problems.

The outlook identifies dehydration, skin disease, nose bleeding, fever, vomiting and breathing difficulties associated with prolonged drought. Reduced access to water for sanitation and hygiene could increase infectious diseases, including typhoid, diarrhoea and lung disease.

Vulnerable people, including people with disabilities in the outer islands, could face reduced access to water. The outlook also warns that hospitals and emergency centres could run out of water if the drought persists.

The effects could extend well beyond households and farms.

The Meteorological Service identifies potential disruption to household incomes and livelihoods, increased demands for drought relief, higher shipping costs and increased pressure on water facilities.

Schools could also be affected, particularly in the outer islands, with reduced water supplies potentially affecting students’ focus and performance. Prolonged drought could lead to lower attendance, dropouts and school closures.

The outlook also warns of an increased risk of wildfires, while power supplies could be disrupted by limited water available for cooling equipment. Fire Services may need to use seawater.

The Meteorological Service notes that the impacts are based on stakeholder consultation and are estimates of when impacts may become evident following below-average rainfall. The severity of impacts can vary according to island size, topography, geology and soil type.

With very dry conditions forecast across every island group and the drought outlook showing further escalation through October, the warning is that Tonga’s dry spell could become a much broader threat to water security, food production, health and livelihoods.

item.title: NZ fur seal stranded on remote Ha'apai island released at sea
item.description: A New Zealand fur seal that was stranded in a remote island in Ha'apai has been released at sea after spending four days in the care of a local fisherman. The rare visitor came ashore on Tokulu, a small limestone island located between the remote islands of Tungua and Nomuka.
item.content:encoded:
A New Zealand fur seal that was stranded in a remote island in Ha'apai has been released at sea after spending four days in the care of a local fisherman.

The rare visitor came ashore on Tokulu, a small limestone island located between the remote islands of Tungua and Nomuka.

Fisherman Sione Meiha’amoa (Toa) told Matangi Tonga that he discovered the juvenile seal stranded on Tokulu last Wednesday, 12 August, and brought it back to his home island of Tungua.

" I found it stranded ashore on Tokulu," Toa said.

The seal remained inland for four days while Toa cared for it before it was released at sea on Sunday, 16 August, to continue its journey.

Toa said a group from New Zealand was contacted through the Prime Minister’s Office to assess the seal. He understood from the group that the animal was about one year old and still a juvenille. He was also told that it had come from New Zealand.

" They were concerned for the animal and wanted me to release it."

Toa said he was told he could face a fine of $10,000 pa'anga if he did not release the seal.

The young fur seal has now been returned to the sea, with hopes that it will make its way back towards its natural habitat.

New Zealand fur seals are not naturally found in Tonga, where tropical waters are far outside the species' usual cold and temperate habitat.

Sightings of seals in Tonga are rare, although similar unusual appearances have been recorded in Tonga, Fiji, Cook Islands, and Tahiti over the years.

The unusual arrival comes as Tonga has experienced periods of colder-than-usual weather in recent months.

The New Zealand Department of Conservation ( DOC ) website states that Kekeno are the most common seals in New Zealand and their population is growing. They are usually found on rocky shores throughout mainland New Zealand, the Chatham Islands, and the subantarctic islands, as well as parts of Australia .

Seals are very good swimmers and weaned pups will sometimes travel great distances. On land seals have been found in unusual places such as backyards, drains and streets.

“Despite these odd appearances, seals are best left alone with no human intervention.”

Fur seals and sea lions are distinguished from other seals by their external ear flaps and hind flippers which rotate forward, allowing them to move quickly on land.

New Zealand fur seals can be distinguished from sea lions by their pointy nose and smaller size.

This pointy-nosed seal has long pale whiskers and a body covered with two layers of fur. Their coat is dark grey-brown on the back, and lighter below.

Adult females grow to a maximum length 1.5 m, weight 30-50 kg, while adult males grow to amaximum length 2.5 m, weight 90-150 kg.

From birth to weaning Pups are suckled for about 300 days, though some will continue to suckle into their second year. During spring most pups are weaned and disperse. Juvenile fur seals have been found over 1000 km away from their place of birth.

item.title: China pushes back on US-led call for advance notice of future missile tests
item.description: Chinese diplomats have pushed back on a joint statement signed by 40 countries, following a Chinese SLBM missile test in the Pacific Islands, with Australia, New Zealand, the Marshall Islands and Palau joining a US -led call for advance notice for future launches. The Chinese say there is a double standard in the demands.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese diplomats have pushed back on a joint statement signed by 40 countries, following a Chinese SLBM missile test in the Pacific Islands, with Australia, New Zealand, the Marshall Islands and Palau joining a US -led call for advance notice for future launches.

The Chinese say there is a double standard in the demands.

China tested a submarine-launched ballistic missile ( SLBM ) into the Pacific Ocean on July 6, 2026. The missile carried a dummy warhead and landed in international open waters in the South Pacific.

The US -led statement of 11 August called for "all relevant countries" to commit to providing no less than 24 hours' notice of launches of intercontinental ballistic missiles and submarine-launched ballistic missiles to affected nations.

Ambassador Li Chijiang, China’s Ambassador for Disarmament Affairs at a Conference on Disarmament last week said the US demand had no legal basis, because t he Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation (“ HCOC ”) is not a universally joined mechanism. “China, as a non-member of the HCOC , is not bound by it.”

However, he said that 24 hours prior to China’s test launch in July this year, China had provided pre-launch notifications to other nuclear-weapon states, including the U.S., Russia, the U.K., and France, as well as Japan, the Republic of Korea, Australia, New Zealand and other Pacific island countries around the missile impact area.

To date, China has conducted only three ICBM launch tests.

He alleged that “The U.S. has conducted over 300 ICBM test launches and about 200 SLBM test launches, and most of its ICBM test launches have taken place in the Pacific Ocean.

“But the U.S. has not provided China with advance notifications in recent years, except on only one occasion.”

The only regional signatories to the US -led statement were Palau, which is hosting the Pacific Islands Forum in September, the Marshall Islands, Australia and New Zealand.

Tonga did not sign the US -led statement and, like other Pacific Islands states, has not overtly criticised the Chinese missile test, while making carefully crafted diplomatic statements..

On 23 July Tonga's Prime Minister Lord Fakafanua highlighted China's duty in Pacific countries to ensure our shared regional environment is one that is “safe and secure”.

He was speaking at a reception in Nuku'alofa to celebrate the 99 th anniversary of Chinese People’s Liberation Army.

Lord Fakafanua said Tonga and the People's Republic of China had enduring diplomatic relations and long standing partnership.

“These ever-shifting ties embody the partnership, its resilience, and transformation while also highlighting China's growing duty in Pacific countries, like Tonga, to ensure our shared regional environment is one that is safe and secure, especially where international peacekeeping and humanitarian support prevails.”

He said Tonga was committed to peaceful dialogue and principled multilateralism, whether through the Pacific Islands Forum, or the United Nations.

“Such multilateral and regional institutions are needed now more than ever. The global uncertainties of today demand that these are the cornerstones of our foreign engagement,” Lord Fakafanua said.

At the function hosted by the Chinese Embassy in Tonga, Ambassador H.E. Liu Weimin, said that China respected the aspirations of regional countries to maintain the South Pacific as a nuclear free zone.
